Every read refolds the two JSONL logs; the fold reports events it could not apply, and export writes a provenance sidecar.

A.best_thing: The fold returns the events it could not apply, with reasons, and log_problems surfaces them (events.py:144-161, ledger.py:109-127): a damaged log is neither fatal nor silently wrong.

generativity.notes: All five reach the same deep shape (stamped label log, append-only decision log, stack fold, queries both ways) and differ in the details, which is what a generative pattern looks like. A, D and E use the chapter's vocabulary (stamper, hashed inputs, schema, sidecar) and differ in packaging: A uses dataclasses and a fold that reports what it ignored; D puts everything in one file and reuses stamp() for export; E has a module per participant but hand-rolls the export stamp. B and C are shaped by the task instead: locks, caches and strict kinds, with no hashing, schema or export lineage. C alone gives the fold the right meaning for multi-round review. Where the chapter said nothing, they split: undo with nothing to undo is recorded by A and D and refused by B, C and E; correct-then-accept keeps the correction only in C (impl-C/labelbook/ledger.py:91-94) and reverts to the proposal in A, B, D and E.

worse_is_better: C is the simplest design with the highest quality: two working modules and no Provenance, Stamp, FoldResult or schema module, yet it is the only one with correct multi-round semantics, safe concurrent appends and a model-check test. Of what the others carry, input hashes and an export sidecar with label ids (A, D, E) are needed for the task's 'audit any exported label' and would cost C about 30 lines. A schema.json (D, E) is cheap and useful. These are not needed: A's Provenance.ids duplicate, unused cache and clock helpers and an in-code SCHEMA that is never written to disk; E's exports.jsonl next to the sidecar and its 23-name public surface; D's and E's MAKER_KINDS lists of preset and program. B is as small as C but drops the lineage forces without gaining anything. D shows the cost of going lean where it matters: no lock or collision-free id, so labels are lost.
chapter_lessons: The sketch's fold (one slot per item; undo deletes it) cannot restore an earlier decision after an undone correction, and all five replaced it with a per-label stack (impl-A/labelbook/events.py:157-164, impl-B/labelbook/events.py:207-219, impl-C/labelbook/ledger.py:392-401, impl-D/labelbook/ledger.py:221-233, impl-E/labelbook/fold.py:40-58). The sketch should show the stack.

The chapter never says what the label in force is after several rounds. Four of five revert to the proposed label when an accept follows a correction (A, B, D, E), and only C keeps the correction (impl-C/labelbook/ledger.py:91-94). This is the 'folds disagree on an edge case' trap occurring across independent implementations. The chapter should define the semantics (the label in force is the last live correction) and recommend a reference-model test like impl-C/tests/test_model_check.py.

'Write the fold once' is not enough: the status vocabulary must be owned by the fold too. B (impl-B/labelbook/ledger.py:152-163) and D (impl-D/labelbook/ledger.py:464) define 'decided' a second time inside acceptance, so a new status such as escalated is silently counted as a rejection. A's catch-all (impl-A/labelbook/events.py:197) folds any new decision as reject.

The readers-vs-writers force also applies to provenance queries. In all five, made_by and acceptance each read the maker on their own, so seeing through an ensemble is a two-site change everywhere. The chapter should name one maker-matching function shared by the lineage queries.

Missing force: identity and atomic appends under concurrent writers. The task's 'a new Ledger on the same directory sees the same state' invites several processes. D's read-then-append sequential ids (impl-D/labelbook/ledger.py:328-337) lose about a third of the labels with 4 writers, while B and C add flock (impl-B/labelbook/store.py:62-80, impl-C/labelbook/storage.py:31-45).

Say outright that derived artefacts such as exports are creating paths. D stamps its export through stamp() (impl-D/labelbook/ledger.py:514-529), E hand-rolls one (impl-E/labelbook/ledger.py:271-279), and B and C export rows that cannot be traced.

Unnecessary as written: the maker-kind list with preset and program was copied into D and E (impl-D/labelbook/ledger.py:49, impl-E/labelbook/provenance.py:21) and never enforced. A schema kept only in code is ornament (impl-A/labelbook/schema.py:21); the note should say the schema must be written beside the data, as D and E do.
